title: The fruit trees in the siege
hookLine: the ban on needless destruction extends to all waste
carry: bal tashchit: no destruction for nothing

cards: An army is camped around a walled city. The siege drags on. The soldiers need wood for ladders and ramps, and all around them stand fruit trees.
The quickest thing would be to cut them all. Deuteronomy stops the axe in mid-air. It's a strange place for an environmental rule, in the middle of a war chapter, but that's where it sits.
And from that one verse about fruit trees, the rabbis grew a principle that reaches into your kitchen, your closet, and even the lamp on your table.

teach.h: THE AXE AND THE FRUIT TREE.
teach.b: Bal tashchit. Do not destroy. First, the verse, which this path met in Shoftim.

During a siege, "thou shalt not destroy the trees thereof by forcing an axe against them." You may eat from them; you may not cut them down. The rabbis' name for the rule echoes that command not to destroy.
Second, the tree's own question. The King James renders a short phrase in the verse as "for the tree of the field is man's life."

Some readers hear the Hebrew as a question instead: is the tree of the field a person, that it should be besieged by you? Either way, the tree isn't the enemy. It feeds the living, and it has no part in the war.
Third, the widening. The Talmud, in tractate Shabbat, says that someone who makes an oil lamp burn faster than it needs to, wasting the oil, transgresses bal tashchit.
Maimonides gathers the principle into law: the same ban applies to one who breaks dishes, tears clothes, wrecks a building, stops up a spring, or ruins food, in a destructive way.

teach.h: A LAMP, A COAT, A MEAL.
teach.b: A fruit tree became a lamp, a coat, a meal. Fourth, the word that matters: needless. The tradition doesn't forbid using things up.
Wood is burned, clothes wear out, food is eaten.
What it forbids is destruction for nothing: waste that serves no one.
The question is whether this use, right now, has a purpose. Even what is truly yours, in this teaching, deserves a reason before the axe.

how: Bal tashchit is studied as a principle of Jewish law, and some Jewish environmental groups and teachers draw on it when they talk about food waste, energy and caring for the earth.

games.q: you're a soldier in a long siege. you need wood, and fruit trees stand all around the city. what does Deuteronomy say?
o: eat from them, but don't cut them down.
burn them so the city can't use them.
games.why: the verse says you may eat from them, but not cut them down. the rabbis built bal tashchit, the ban on needless destruction, on it.

practice: Walk through your day in your mind: the fridge, the tap, the lights left on, the clothes you've stopped wearing, the packaging, the leftovers. Let one waste stand out, something that serves no one, and pick just that one.
Decide how you'll handle it, eat the leftover, turn off the light, mend the shirt, concrete enough that tonight you'll know.

wordCard.voice: Bal tashchit. Do not destroy: a rule about fruit trees in a siege, widened by the rabbis to all needless waste. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: do not destroy. From Deuteronomy 20:19.
